question: What images of animals and of family does the LORD use, right at the opening, to describe Israel's relationship with Him?
Why does God reject sacrifices, feasts and prayers that the Law itself provided for, and what does He ask for in their place?
The word מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, “justice”) appears in the appeal, in the lament and in the promise of the chapter: what relationship does it have with the orphan, the widow and the future of Zion?
“Come now, let us reason together”: what changes for you in knowing that God invites you to a conversation about your own sins?
According to the vision, what will the nations seek on the mountain of the LORD, and what happens to the swords and spears?
Cedars, mountains, towers, walls and ships of Tarshish: why does the “day of the LORD” turn against all these lofty things?
The verb שָׁפֵל (shafel, “bring low, humble”) is repeated alongside “exalted”: what contrast does the chapter build between human beings and the LORD?
“Put no more trust in man, who has only the breath in his nostrils”: in whom or what do you usually place the trust the text reserves for God?
What kinds of leaders and support does the Lord promise to take away from Jerusalem, and what disorder takes their place?
Why does the accusation against the elders and leaders speak of a devoured vineyard and of grinding the faces of the poor?
The verb מָשַׁל (mashal, “rule”) describes those who govern the people in verses 4 and 12: what portrait of Judah's leadership does the prophet paint?
How is the long list of the daughters of Zion's finery linked to the denunciation of the oppression of the poor made just before?
The verses about the righteous and the wicked appear in the middle of a collective crisis: what do they say to you when everything around seems to collapse?
Who will be called “holy” in Jerusalem, and what will the Lord have to wash and cleanse before that?
The cloud by day and the fire by night recall what episode in Israel's history, and what does this image promise for Zion?
The word צֶמַח (tsemach, “Branch, sprout”) comes from the world of plants: what does it suggest here, right after the judgment, and how have Jewish and Christian interpreters read it?
God is described as a canopy, shade and refuge from the storm: what shelter do you need at this stage of life?
What did the owner do for the vineyard, what did he expect from it, and what does he decide to do when it yields worthless grapes?

In verse 7, מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, “justice”) sounds almost the same as the word for “bloodshed,” and “righteousness” almost the same as “cry”: what does this play of sounds highlight about the vineyard owner's disappointment?
The “woes” of the chapter denounce what behaviors, and what connection do they have with the vineyard that yielded bad grapes?
“Woe to those who call evil good and good evil”: where do you notice this exchange of names happening today, including in yourself?
What does Isaiah see and hear in the temple, and how do the seraphim behave before the Lord?
The word קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh, “holy”) is said three times by the seraphim: what does this repetition convey, and how is it linked to the title “Holy One of Israel,” so frequent in the book?
What steps take Isaiah from “Woe is me” to “Here am I. Send me!”?
How should we understand a mission to a people who will not listen, and what does the image of the stump left after the felling leave open?
Faced with the question “Whom shall I send?”, what weighs on you when it comes to answering a call?
What political crisis frightens Ahaz and the house of David, and what does the LORD tell Isaiah to say to the king?

In verse 9 there is a play on the verb אָמַן (aman, “believe, be firm”): “If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.” What link does the prophet make between trusting and remaining standing?
The word עַלְמָה (almah), translated here as “virgin,” designates a young woman: how have Jewish and Christian readings understood this sign, and what did it say to Ahaz at that moment?
Why does Ahaz refuse to ask for a sign, and how does the time frame tied to the boy in verse 16 place the sign within the crisis of that period?
“Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid”: in the face of what threats do you need to hear these words today?
What does the name given to the prophet's son mean, and what event does this name announce?
What contrast does the prophet draw between the waters of Shiloah, “that flow gently,” and the waters of the river that flood Judah?
The word מִקְדָּשׁ (miqdash, “sanctuary”) appears together with “stone of stumbling”: how can the same LORD be a refuge for some and a fall for others?
“Do not fear what they fear”: what collective fears of your time compete with the fear of God?
What regions are mentioned at the beginning of the chapter, and what change from darkness to light is announced to them?
How have Jewish and Christian readers understood the names given to the child in verse 6, and what link does verse 7 make with the throne of David?
The child is called “Prince of Peace,” and the peace of His government “will have no end”: what senses of שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace, well-being”) fit in this promise?
The refrain “yet for all this, His anger is not turned away” is repeated: what attitudes of Israel does the prophet denounce between one repetition and the next?
“The bricks have fallen, but we will rebuild with finished stone”: when do you react to a loss without asking what it has to teach?
Against whom is the “woe” at the beginning of the chapter, and what practices are denounced?
Assyria is called “the rod of My anger”: what does the image of the axe and the saw say about an instrument that boasts as if it were the author?
The word שְׁאָר (she’ar, “remnant”) recalls the name of Isaiah's son, Shear-jashub (7:3): what hope and what limit does the theme of the remnant bring here?
The king of Assyria says “by the strength of my hand I have done this, and by my wisdom”: in what achievements of yours do you risk thinking this way?
From where does the “shoot” of verse 1 spring, and what gifts of the Spirit of the LORD rest upon it?

The word נֵצֶר (netser, “branch, shoot”) comes from the roots of a cut stump: what does this image say about the hope of the house of David after the judgment, and how have Jews and Christians read this promise?
What kind of judge does the text describe, and why does he not judge “by what his eyes see”?
Wolf with lamb, child with serpent: how do you understand this peace that reaches even the animals, and what explanation does verse 9 offer for it?
What small sign of this peace between enemies could you help bring about in the place where you live?
What change does the singer describe in the relationship between himself and the LORD?
The word יְשׁוּעָה (yeshu‘ah, “salvation”) appears twice, and the second time with the image of the springs: what sense of salvation does this song suggest?
Why must Israel's thanksgiving be proclaimed “among the peoples” and “throughout the earth”?
“Although You were angry with me... You have comforted me”: what experience of comfort, after a hard time, could you turn into a song?
To whom is this oracle addressed, and how is the army the LORD summons described?
Sun, moon and stars grow dark on the “day of the LORD”: what does this cosmic language mean when applied to the fall of an empire?
The word גָּאוֹן (ga’on, “pride, arrogance”) appears in the punishment of the world and in the description of Babylon: why is pride at the center of the accusation?
Verses 15-18 describe terrible violence against children and women: how can we read such a text honestly, without softening it or taking it as a model?
Babylon, “the jewel of the kingdoms,” ends up inhabited by jackals: what human security seems eternal to you and perhaps is not?
Who sings the taunt against the king of Babylon, and how do the earth, the cedars and the dead in Sheol react?

The word הֵילֵל (helel, “shining one”), linked to the “son of the dawn,” has been read in very different ways throughout history: what does it mean in the context of a song against the king of Babylon?
What ambitions does the king express with his “I will ascend,” and what contrast is there between these ascents and the place where he ends up?
After the oracles against Babylon, Assyria and Philistia, what place does verse 32 give to Zion and to the afflicted of the people?
Where does the desire to be “above” others appear in your life, and how does it resemble this king's speech?
What cities of Moab are mentioned, and what gestures of mourning do the people make?
Why does the prophet say “my heart cries out over Moab,” if this is an oracle about a neighboring nation and an old rival of Israel?
The word בְּכִי (bekhi, “weeping”) is repeated along with many cries and laments: what effect does this accumulation produce on the reader?
How do you usually react when someone who was your adversary goes through suffering?
What request is made on behalf of Moab's fugitives, and what promise of a throne appears in the middle of the oracle?

The throne “will be established in loving devotion”: the word חֶסֶד (chesed, “loyal kindness”) comes together with faithfulness, justice and righteousness. What kind of government does this combination describe?
How does the chapter bring together the denunciation of Moab's pride and the prophet's weeping for the vines of Sibmah and Heshbon?
“Hide the refugees; do not betray the one who flees”: what responsibility does this request suggest toward the refugees of today?
What cities and kingdoms are struck in this oracle, and why does Ephraim appear alongside Damascus?
What do the images of the harvest and of the few olives left at the top of the tree say about Israel's destiny?
The verb שָׁעָה (sha‘ah, “look, give attention”) appears in verses 7 and 8: from what does the human gaze turn away, and to whom does it turn?
“You have forgotten the God of your salvation”: what has led you to forget who your rock and your refuge is?
How does the text describe the land beyond the rivers of Cush and the people who send envoys by sea?
The LORD watches “quietly,” like heat and dew, and then prunes the vines: what do these images suggest about the way He acts in history?
The word שַׁי (shai, “gift, offering”) appears at the end: what changes in the relationship between this distant people and Mount Zion from the beginning to the end of the chapter?
God says He will “quietly look on from My dwelling place”: how do you get through the times when God seems not to act?
What areas of Egypt's life are struck by the judgment in verses 1-10?
Why does the prophet mock the princes of Zoan and Pharaoh's “wise” counselors?
The verb רָפָא (rafa’, “heal”) comes together with “strike” in verse 22: how does this pair help us understand the purpose of the judgment on Egypt?
What surprising change does the end of the chapter announce for Egypt and Assyria, and what place does Israel have between the two?
“Blessed be Egypt My people”: whom do you find it hard to imagine as someone blessed by God?
What gesture is Isaiah ordered to make, and to what political event is it linked?
Why is the sign addressed to those who put their hope in Egypt and in Cush?
The word עָרוֹם (arom, “naked”) is repeated in verses 2-4: what did the prophet's nakedness communicate in a world where prisoners of war were led away like that?
“See what has happened to those we relied on”: what support you trusted has already collapsed, and what did that teach you?
What task does the watchman receive, and what news does he finally announce?
Why does the prophet react with pain and horror at the vision of the fall of an oppressive empire?
The question put to the watchman, from the verb שָׁמַר (shamar, “watch, guard”), “what is left of the night?”, receives an enigmatic answer: what meaning do you see in it?
“If you would inquire, then inquire. Come back yet again”: what question about your own “night” do you still need to ask?
What was Shebna preparing for himself, and what does the LORD announce about him and about Eliakim?
The verb נָבַט (navat, “look, pay attention”) appears in verses 8 and 11: where did Jerusalem look in the face of danger, and where did it stop looking?
The Lord calls for weeping, and the people answer “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die”: what does this reaction reveal about the city?
The key of the house of David and the peg driven into a firm place: what do these images say about authority, and why does even the firm peg end up falling?
“You did not look to the One who made it”: in what plans of yours do you take care of everything except looking to God?
What cities and regions appear in the lament over Tyre, and where did its wealth come from?
Who decreed the fall of Tyre, according to the text, and for what purpose?
The verb זָנָה (zanah, “prostitute oneself”) is used for Tyre's trade: why does the prophet choose this image to speak of wealth and of relations between kingdoms?
In the end, Tyre's profit is “set apart for the LORD” and feeds others: what does this turn suggest about the destiny of the money you earn?
What pairs of people does verse 2 list, and what happens to all of them?
The verb פָּרַר (parar, “break, annul”) describes what the inhabitants did with the “everlasting covenant”: what link does the text make between human guilt and the defilement of the earth?
Why, while songs are heard from the ends of the earth, does the prophet say “I waste away, I waste away. Woe is me”?
What does the end of the chapter announce about the host “on high” and the kings of the earth, and who will reign in Zion?
The text links people's way of life to the state of the earth itself: what relationship do you see between your choices and the world around you?
Why does the singer praise the LORD, and how is God described in relation to the poor and the needy?
Who are the guests at the banquet on the mountain, and what will the LORD do there with the veil that covers the peoples?
The verb בָּלַע (bala‘, “devour, swallow”) is used for the veil over the peoples and for death itself: what does it mean to say that the great devourer will be devoured?
“The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face”: what tears, yours or other people's, do you entrust to this promise?
What city is celebrated in the song, and what other city is brought down to the dust?
In verse 3, “perfect peace” translates the word שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace”) said twice: what does this repetition add, and to whom is this peace promised?
Verse 14 says the dead “will not rise,” and verse 19 that “your dead will live”: how should we understand this contrast, and how has this hope been read in Judaism and Christianity?
What does the image of the woman in labor who gives birth only to wind express about the people's efforts?
“My soul longs for You in the night”: at what moments do you seek God with this kind of longing?
Leviathan (לִוְיָתָן, livyatan), the coiling serpent and dragon of the sea, comes from ancient images of chaos: what does it mean to say the LORD will slay him “in that day”?
Compare this song of the vineyard with that of Isaiah 5: what has changed in the owner's attitude toward the vineyard?
What does the great trumpet announce at the end of the chapter, and from where do those who were perishing return?
“Let them make peace with Me”: what reconciliation, with God or with someone, have you been putting off?
Who are the “drunkards of Ephraim,” and what leaders of Judah also appear staggering from wine?
The phrase “order on order, line on line” imitates speech: how does it sound in the mouth of the scoffers, and how does it turn against them?

The stone (אֶבֶן, even) laid in Zion is tested, precious and a cornerstone: what contrast does it make with the “covenant with death” of verses 15 and 18, and how was it later read by Jews and Christians?
What does the parable of the farmer, who does not treat all grains the same way, teach about the way God acts?
“The one who believes will never be shaken”: in what decision of yours has haste taken the place of trust?
Who is Ariel, and what happens, according to verses 7-8, to the nations that fight against her?
What situation does the image of the sealed book, which neither the literate nor the illiterate can read, describe?
The verb יָצַר (yatsar, “form”), used for the potter, appears in verse 16: what is at stake when the work says of the one who formed it, “He has no understanding”?
What reversals do verses 17-24 announce for the deaf, the blind, the humble and the needy?
“These people draw near to Me with their mouths... but their hearts are far from Me”: where does your devotion risk staying only on your lips?
What alliance does Judah seek without consulting the LORD, and what name does God give Egypt in verse 7?
What do the people ask of the seers and prophets, and why do they want to stop “confronting us with the Holy One of Israel”?
The word שׁוּבָה (shuvah, “return, repentance”) appears together with rest, quietness and trust: what path of strength does verse 15 propose, different from the horses of verse 16?
Verse 18 says the LORD “longs to be gracious”: what image of God emerges in verses 18-21, after so much accusation?
“This is the way; walk in it”: at what crossroads would you like to hear this voice, and how do you usually seek it?
In what do those who go down to Egypt trust, and whom do they fail to seek?
Verse 3 sets flesh (בָּשָׂר, basar) against spirit: what does this opposition say about Egypt's help and about God's help?
The lion that is not intimidated and the birds hovering over the nest: how do these two images of the LORD complement each other?
“Return to the One against whom you have so blatantly rebelled”: what does it mean for you to come back after having sought other supports?
How are the righteous king and princes described, and what difference does the text make between the fool, the scoundrel and the noble?
Why are the women “so secure” called to tremble, and what will happen to the fields and the city?
The word צְדָקָה (tsedaqah, “righteousness”) appears after the Spirit is poured out from on high: what relationship does the text establish between righteousness, peace and security?
“Each will be like a shelter from the wind”: for whom could you be a shelter, shade or water this week?
Against whom is the “woe” of verse 1, and what do the people ask of the LORD in verse 2?
How do verses 15-16 answer the question “who among us can dwell with a consuming fire?”, and what stands out in the attitudes described?
Verse 22 gives the LORD three titles, beginning with judge, from the verb שָׁפַט (shafat, “judge”): what does it mean to unite in one person the roles of judging, lawgiving and reigning?
“Be our strength every morning”: what do you ask of God at the beginning of your days?
Whom does the chapter summon to listen, and what people is named as the specific target of the judgment?
The sword “drunk” in heaven and the sacrifice in Bozrah: how should we read such extreme images of violence against Edom, remembering the long history between Edom and Israel?
The measuring line (קַו, qav), which in 28:17 measures with justice, appears again in verses 11 and 17: what does it measure here, and for whom is the land divided at the end?
“Search the scroll of the LORD and read”: what place does attentive reading of Scripture have in your questions about justice and judgment?
What transformations happen to the desert, and what will be seen in it?
The blind, the deaf, the lame and the mute are healed: what relationship is there between these healings and the waters that gush forth in the wilderness?
The “Highway of Holiness” translates דֶּרֶךְ (derekh, “way, road”): who walks on it and where does it lead, according to verses 8-10?
“Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees”: to whom can you say “do not fear” in these days?
At what moment in Judah's history does the chapter take place, and who goes out to meet the Rabshakeh?
The verb בָּטַח (batach, “trust”) is repeated in the Rabshakeh's speech: what trusts does he try to knock down, one by one?
Why do the officials ask the Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic, and why does he insist on speaking in Hebrew to the people on the wall?
What argument does the Rabshakeh draw from the defeat of the gods of the nations, and how does the book of Isaiah answer this reasoning?
The people stay silent by the king's order: in what situations is silence in the face of provocation the wisest answer for you?
What does Hezekiah do on hearing the Rabshakeh's words, and what answer does he receive through Isaiah?
Hezekiah spreads the letter out “before the LORD”: what does his prayer affirm about God and about the gods of the nations, and what is the final aim of the request?
The verb חָרַף (charaf, “taunt, defy”) appears in Hezekiah's plea and in God's answer: against whom, after all, was the king of Assyria's taunt directed?
What does the LORD tell the king of Assyria about who planned his victories, and what image does He use to describe his return?
When threatening news arrives, what would it mean for you to “spread it out before the LORD,” as Hezekiah did?
What news does Hezekiah receive, how does he react, and what sign accompanies God's answer?
What images does Hezekiah use in his song to describe the nearness of death?
The verb חָיָה (chayah, “live”) and the word “living” run through the song: what value does life gain in verses 16-19, and why is it said that Sheol “cannot praise You”?
“Surely for my own welfare I had such great anguish”: looking back, what difficulty of yours do you now see differently?
Who visits Hezekiah, for what reason, and what does the king show the envoys?
The text says Hezekiah was pleased (שָׂמַח, samach) with the envoys: what does this joy reveal about where the king was seeking recognition and support?
Why does showing the treasures to the envoys of Babylon provoke such a grave announcement, and how does it prepare the second part of the book?
Hezekiah takes comfort in “there will be peace and security in my lifetime”: how do you think about the consequences of your choices for those who will come after?
What change of tone does this chapter bring in relation to the previous one, and what must be spoken “tenderly to Jerusalem”?
What way does the voice command to be prepared in the wilderness, and what meaning did this image have for exiles who hoped to return home?
The word חָצִיר (chatsir, “grass”) is repeated three times: what contrast does the text set up between human frailty and the word of God?
The questions “who has measured...?” and “to whom will you liken God?” pile up: what do they want to provoke in a people who say “my way is hidden from the LORD”?
“Those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength”: in what area of life are you weary, and what would it mean to wait on the LORD there?
